Prescribed minimum benefits

By: Este de Klerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Prescribed Minimum Benefits are intended to help those who are at their sickest and most vulnerable - but is the legislation doing what it's intended?

Unique Selling Point:
You are an ordinary middle class South African with a full time job and two kids. Every month, when your salary comes in, and those debit orders go out, medical aid premiums are a large chunk of the monthly expenses you bear. It might be barely affordable but many people will continue to pay just in case - for that day when the dread diagnosis of cancer comes, or you are admitted to hospital. When that day comes, you'll be relying on your medical aid to cover you - and the legislation is on your side. By law, emergencies, 25 chronic conditions and a list of 270 other conditions are covered as Prescribed Minimum Benefits for anyone who is a medical aid scheme member. But will you really reap those benefits when the time comes? Thanks to inadequately enforced regulations and medical aids failing to inform their members of their rights, many South Africans are paying out of pocket...which can mean losing your job, your car and ending up in debt review for hundreds of thousands. A new Competition Commission inquiry backs up what many doctors and patients have been saying for years. Carte Blanche takes a dive into the world of medical care to find out what's going wrong.

Summary:
Anyone who can afford to, pays ever-increasing medical aid premiums as a safety net for the day that the worst happens and you are diagnosed with cancer or a chronic condition. 16% of the South African population is covered by private medical aid care. In 1998 legislation was gazetted to implement Prescribed Minimum Benefits: a list of chronic, emergency and acute conditions which must be covered in full for any patient who is on a medical aid. This was supposed to be just the beginning of a series of policies to regulate the medical aid industry, but 20 years later the list has never been updated and neither have the treatment protocols. To make matters worse, most medical aid companies fail to inform their members that their conditions should be covered as PMBs. The result is patients paying extortionate medical expenses out of pocket, often when they are already incapacitated by illness. And for the rest of us, rising premiums making medical aid care ever less affordable and less comprehensive.

Further information:
How the medical aid system works: the intention is that healthy and younger members subsidise older and sicker ones. We all pay our premiums; part of them is set aside for your savings pocket, to be used by you for everyday expenditure at your discretion. The rest is put into a risk pool, from which PMB expenses are paid. If you are diagnosed with a PMB condition, you are usually required to apply for a PMB benefit, but medical aid companies also have a legal obligation to proactively advise members that they qualify. However, patients frequently pay their PMB medical expenses out of their savings accounts, which are rapidly depleted, and are none the wiser about the systems that should be supporting them.

In 2013, the Competition Commission approved an investigation into anti-competitive behaviour within the medical aid scheme industry. The preliminary Health Market Inquiry report, released earlier this year, found that:
- there has been a chronic failure of implementation by the Department of Health, CMS and other regulators in the industry, and intended revisions and additions to the legislation have not been implemented since 2000
- the market is characterised by rising costs and disempowered consumers who are not adequately informed to navigate the system
- private healthcare expenditure is high and has been increasing at a rate above CPI
- lack of clarity on PMB cover amongst both healthcare practitioners and members means that treatment is a matter of trial and error; and the drive to access coverage means doctors might prescribe unnecessarily expensive treatment, or admit patients to hospital unnecessarily.
- there are no mechanisms to ensure compliance by medical aids on PMB payments
- prices are high because before 2004 tariffs were decided by collective bargaining; thereafter by inflation which never corrected for the excessive costs in 2004 when the change happened.
- The WHO found that South Africa has one of the most expensive private healthcare systems in the world
- At every step, it is patients and medical aid scheme members who bear the brunt of increasing costs and lowering coverage.

We will speak to an expert Dr van Loggerenberg, who is a GP with an MBA in medical aid schemes. He is outspoken and critical, and very well informed about the systems. He will tell us

Charl du Toit Depression sufferer

PRESCRIBED MINIMUM BENEFITS
PRODUCER: ESTÉ DE KLERK
RESEARCHER/JOURNALIST: LAURA BYRNE
PRESENTER: DEVI SANKAREE GOVENDER
EDITOR: ROBIN LEUCI
BROADCAST DATE: 16 SEPTEMBER 2018

VO: Every month you fork out thousands of rands, trusting that if you're in an accident, or you're diagnosed with sudden illness, your medical aid will take care of the bills that quickly pile up. By law they should, but it might come down to how hard you'll be able fight.

Durban businesswoman Linda Algie didn't know her rights when her husband Simon Spencer caught his foot in a ladder and fell last year.

LINDA ALGIE: Both his tibia and fibula had snapped and a lot of ankle bones were just gone,

VO: Simon was hospitalized, had two orthopaedic surgeries, and a long recovery at home. His diagnosis was an "open fracture and dislocation of bones and joints" - a diagnosis that's covered by prescribed minimum benefits or PMBs.

DEVI LINK: it's a set of defined benefits to ensure that all medical scheme members have access to certain health services, regardless of the benefit option they have selected.

VO: The Medical Schemes Act of 1998 mandated medical schemes to pay for PMB conditions since 2000, says the National Health Department's Dr Anban Pillay.

DR ANBAN PILLAY: it was also to prevent medical schemes from them passing those patients back onto the State once they have exhausted their benefits

VO: PMBs were defined into three categories:
25 chronic diseases including illnesses like diabetes and epilepsy;
270 acute conditions such as strokes that are mostly treated in-hospital;
and some emergency medical conditions.

Medical aid schemes are supposed to help patients access medical care through a mutual fund. Every month members pay their premiums of which a portion goes into a personal savings account - if your plan has one. The rest goes into a shared risk pool, from which PMBs should be paid.

DEVI LINK 1: The idea is that younger and healthier members would claim less and subsidise older and ill members who tend to make more claims.

DR ANBAN PILLAY: the understanding was that people would use the State for primary benefits and get covered for the catastrophic benefits through the PMB's and get private cover for that.

VO: But state healthcare has been crippled and private healthcare has become increasingly expensive and complicated.

DEVI LINK: many members don't even know what a PMB is …. And when you do find out that your condition is a pmb, claiming from your medical aid is not a simple process.

Dr Darian van Loggrenberg has done extensive research on PMBs.

DR DARIAN VAN LOGGRENBERG: Currently there are about 88 medical schemes. Each one has about ten different options, each one with its own rules

LINDA: I got an email from the orthopaedic surgeon with an invoice for 79 thousand rand. I was horrified. I discovered that there was 377 thousand rand outstanding that the medical aid hadn't settled.

VO: Linda says their medical aid tried everything to avoid paying.

LINDA ALGIE: they couldn't cover us because of the plan we were on, or because we had used a provider that was out of Network, or the service providers used the wrong codes.

VO: Linda had to fight for every cent they were owed.

LINDA: I had to become an expert on NAPPI codes, ICD10 codes, procedure codes. I looked at court cases. If you didn't know the law then the medical aid could quite easily bamboozle you.

VO: Amid soaring costs and badly implemented PMBs, the Competition Commission was tasked to investigate private healthcare. In July the 5-year long Health Market Inquiry released a preliminary report, saying the industry was characterised by rising costs, uninformed consumers and a lack of accountability.

DEVI LINK: The Competition Commission found that the PMB structure hasn't been reviewed since its introduction 18 years ago. Yet, the National Department of Health is legally obliged to do so every two years.

VO: Dr Pillay says part of the problem seems to be which conditions are included.

DR ANBAN PILLAY: members of medical schemes are aggrieved about where their condition is not reflected on the PMB's. There would be no legal justification for us to leave one or other condition out.

VO: Dr Sipho Kabane is the CEO of the Council for Medical Schemes which regulates the industry.

DR SIPHO KABANE: what the Minister has picked up and discussed with the CMS, he was not happy with the way the PMB's were constructed in the first place. a lot of this list and conditions that we put as PMB's were more hospital-based. there was no mention of disease prevention and health promotion.

DR DARIAN VAN LOGGRENBERG: Schemes do not have to pay for treatment of osteoporosis, but they will pay for the fracture after you've fallen and broken your hip.

VO: Chronic depression is another condition not included on the list. "Jo" was clinically diagnosed in his early 30s.

DEVI TO "JO": Why did you want us to hide your identity?

"JO": I'll feel judged.

DEVI TO "JO": How many suicide attempts did you make?

"JO": My most recent actual attempt was in 2010 and my first attempt was in my matric year. And then in between there's been a few attempts.

VO: Chronic depression is not covered by PMBs. So, Jo has to pay for antidepressants from his savings, which are depleted by June. He ends up paying R2000 for medication in addition to his R4600 medical aid premium.

"JO": I have stopped taking the medication at one stage, around 2011. I just become almost internally catatonic.

DEVI TO "JO": Does that frighten you?

"JO": I would go to a park, find a tree, decide if I can hang from this tree. So that becomes your 24/7 thinking.

VO: Dr Pillay says if the PMB list was to be updated, costs for consumers would rise even more.

DR ANBAN PILLAY: a household that's earning R20 000 a month, is paying on average about 3800 a month for their medical, which is about 20 percent. By 2030, we're estimating that a third of their income will actually be used for medical scheme premium.

VO: Some schemes illegally pay PMB claims from savings accounts instead of the risk pool. This is the case for Tonya Khoury and her mom Dee. Dee's been ill for 15 years with several conditions of which three are covered by chronic PMBs: Systemic Lupus Erythematosis, Parkinson's Disease and Hypothyroidism.

TONYA KHOURY: The medical aid wasn't paying for the full fees for the doctor. The medical aid wasn't paying for the medication. We were in five, six thousand rand a month worth of debt for just medication.

DEVI TO DEE: How have the medical costs over the past few years impacted on your life.
DEE KHOURY: it's been terrible. I lost my home in Benoni, because I couldn't manage the expenses anymore.

DEVI TO DEE: And you took out one of the top plans.

DEE KHOURY: … their top plan.

TONYA: So the bill would come back from the medical aid. So I phoned them. And, Devi, it took forever to speak to somebody who understood what a PMB was. That person then told me that they only pay R580 towards a specialist on a PMB condition like Lupus.

VO: Tonya asked the medical aid to find her a specialist physician in Gauteng who only charged R580. They couldn't.

TONYA KHOURY: I went to the medical aid and I took a broker from another medical aid, and we sat in their offices until we were heard. And ultimately they agreed to pay the full consultation fee. but what else aren't they paying for? So then I went back and I said,It needs to be backdated to the day when she was diagnosed with the condition. They gave me a year.

VO: Dee's medication costs have not been resolved.

DEVI TO DEE: But now out of pocket per month, you're paying around what?
DEE KHOURY: about R5 000 a month.
VO: The CMS should regulate medical schemes' actions, but Dr Kabane says they have limited resources to pit against medical schemes with seemingly unlimited funds.

DR SIPHO KABANE: There are fines that are stipulated in the Act. We don't think they are sufficient. you get schemes that do this repeatedly. currently people write their own rules that are contrary to the Medical Schemes Act. They use their own rules to conduct these illegal practises.

DEVI: In which world is that OK?

DR SIPHO KABANE: It's not OK in our world. We will be taking stronger action, even if it means us taking them to court.

VO: Even when your medical aid agrees to cover your condition under PMBs, protocols dictate treatment and medication.

DR DARIAN VAN LOGGRENBERG: each condition has a list of treatments associated with it, and each of those treatments has a list of drugs that you're allowed to use and that drug list is called the formulary.

DR ANBAN PILLAY: there is no legislated list of what would be covered under each condition. The minimum list is what the Department of Health determines as the standard treatment guidelines

DR DARIAN VAN LOGGRENBERG: schemes are allowed to draw up their own formularies, with the caveat being that it has to be at least equal the level of service that they would get from a government institution.

VO: This means that all your medical scheme is obliged to pay is the treatment and medication you would receive for free in a government hospital.

DEVI: Then why am I paying for private medical aid?

DR DARIAN VAN LOGGRENBERG: Why are you? We live in the 21st century where we've got amazing tech all around us. But healthcare is being based on the lowest possible denominator.

VO: The Health Department and CMS say they are taking steps to improve the situation - but after 20 years, it is still up to consumers to speak up, or fight, like Linda did when she laid a complaint with the CMS. Her medical aid eventually paid every cent of the outstanding bills.

LINDA: I've learnt that medical aids aren't in the business of helping people. They are in the business of making money. my husband was really ill. There is no way he would have been able to take on this job.


PROMOS

PROMO 1: 30"

As a private medical aid member, you fork out thousands of rands monthly, believing you'll be protected in case of that accident or dread disease. And by law, you should be fully covered for conditions known as prescribed minimum benefits. But how hard are you prepared to fight for your rights?

TONYA KHOURY: The medical aid wasn't paying for the full fees for the doctor. The medical aid wasn't paying for the medication. And the next thing we knew, we were in five, six thousand rand a month worth of debt

LINDA: If you didn't know the law then the medical aid could quite easily bamboozle you and say, "No, we're not liable."

PROMO 2:15"

In 2000, Prescribed Minimum Benefits were defined by law listing medical conditions that should be fully covered by medical schemes. But in most cases, unless you put up a fight, it's simply not happening.

LINDA: if they're not paying, they're winning.

PROMO 3: 15"

Prescribed Minimum Benefits cover medical conditions that schemes have to pay in full. Signed into law 18 years ago, the list of PMB conditions was supposed to have been updated every two years. Carte Blanche finds out why this never happened.

PROMO 4: 10"

Prescribed Minimum Benefits were designed to ensure that all medical aid members get access to basic care…but many are without the cover they pay for.

DR ANBAN PILLAY: a household that's earning R20 000 a month, is paying on average about 3800 a month for their medical, which is about 20 percent. By 2030, we're estimating that a third of their income will actually be used for medical scheme premium. VO: Some schemes illegally pay PMB claims from savings accounts instead of the risk pool. This is the case for Tonya Khoury and her mom Dee. Dee's been ill for 15 years with several conditions of which three are covered by chronic PMBs: Systemic Lupus Erythematosis, Parkinson's Disease and Hypothyroidism. TONYA KHOURY: The medical aid wasn't paying for the full fees for the doctor. The medical aid wasn't paying for the medication. We were in five, six thousand rand a month worth of debt for just medication. DEVI TO DEE: How have the medical costs over the past few years impacted on your life. DEE KHOURY: it's been terrible. I lost my home in Benoni, because I couldn't manage the expenses anymore. DEVI TO DEE: And you took out one of the top plans. DEE KHOURY: … their top plan. TONYA: So the bill would come back from the medical aid. So I phoned them. And, Devi, it took forever to speak to somebody who understood what a PMB was. That person then told me that they only pay R580 towards a specialist on a PMB condition like Lupus. VO: Tonya asked the medical aid to find her a specialist physician in Gauteng who only charged R580. They couldn't. TONYA KHOURY: I went to the medical aid and I took a broker from another medical aid, and we sat in their offices until we were heard. And ultimately they agreed to pay the full consultation fee. but what else aren't they paying for? So then I went back and I said,It needs to be backdated to the day when she was diagnosed with the condition. They gave me a year. VO: Dee's medication costs have not been resolved. DEVI TO DEE: But now out of pocket per month, you're paying around what? DEE KHOURY: about R5 000 a month. VO: The CMS should regulate medical schemes' actions, but Dr Kabane says they have limited resources to pit against medical schemes with seemingly unlimited funds. DR SIPHO KABANE: There are fines that are stipulated in the Act. We don't think they are sufficient. you get schemes that do this repeatedly. currently people write their own rules that are contrary to the Medical Schemes Act. They use their own rules to conduct these illegal practises. DEVI: In which world is that OK? DR SIPHO KABANE: It's not OK in our world. We will be taking stronger action, even if it means us taking them to court. VO: Even when your medical aid agrees to cover your condition under PMBs, protocols dictate treatment and medication. DR DARIAN VAN LOGGRENBERG: each condition has a list of treatments associated with it, and each of those treatments has a list of drugs that you're allowed to use and that drug list is called the formulary. DR ANBAN PILLAY: there is no legislated list of what would be covered under each condition. The minimum list is what the Department of Health determines as the standard treatment guidelines DR DARIAN VAN LOGGRENBERG: schemes are allowed to draw up their own formularies, with the caveat being that it has to be at least equal the level of service that they would get from a government institution. VO: This means that all your medical scheme is obliged to pay is the treatment and medication you would receive for free in a government hospital. DEVI: Then why am I paying for private medical aid? DR DARIAN VAN LOGGRENBERG: Why are you? We live in the 21st century where we've got amazing tech all around us. But healthcare is being based on the lowest possible denominator. VO: The Health Department and CMS say they are taking steps to improve the situation - but after 20 years, it is still up to consumers to speak up, or fight, like Linda did when she laid a complaint with the CMS. Her medical aid eventually paid every cent of the outstanding bills. LINDA: I've learnt that medical aids aren't in the business of helping people. They are in the business of making money. my husband was really ill. There is no way he would have been able to take on this job. PROMOS PROMO 1: 30" As a private medical aid member, you fork out thousands of rands monthly, believing you'll be protected in case of that accident or dread disease. And by law, you should be fully covered for conditions known as prescribed minimum benefits. But how hard are you prepared to fight for your rights? TONYA KHOURY: The medical aid wasn't paying for the full fees for the doctor. The medical aid wasn't paying for the medication. And the next thing we knew, we were in five, six thousand rand a month worth of debt LINDA: If you didn't know the law then the medical aid could quite easily bamboozle you and say, "No, we're not liable." PROMO 2:15" In 2000, Prescribed Minimum Benefits were defined by law listing medical conditions that should be fully covered by medical schemes. But in most cases, unless you put up a fight, it's simply not happening. LINDA: if they're not paying, they're winning. PROMO 3: 15" Prescribed Minimum Benefits cover medical conditions that schemes have to pay in full. Signed into law 18 years ago, the list of PMB conditions was supposed to have been updated every two years. Carte Blanche finds out why this never happened. PROMO 4: 10" Prescribed Minimum Benefits were designed to ensure that all medical aid members get access to basic care…but many are without the cover they pay for.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Prescribed Minimum Benefits are intended to help those who are at their sickest and most vulnerable - but is the legislation doing what it's intended?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: You are an ordinary middle class South African with a full time job and two kids. Every month, when your salary comes in, and those debit orders go out, medical aid premiums are a large chunk of the monthly expenses you bear. It might be barely affordable but many people will continue to pay just in case - for that day when the dread diagnosis of cancer comes, or you are admitted to hospital. When that day comes, you'll be relying on your medical aid to cover you - and the legislation is on your side. By law, emergencies, 25 chronic conditions and a list of 270 other conditions are covered as Prescribed Minimum Benefits for anyone who is a medical aid scheme member. But will you really reap those benefits when the time comes? Thanks to inadequately enforced regulations and medical aids failing to inform their members of their rights, many South Africans are paying out of pocket...which can mean losing your job, your car and ending up in debt review for hundreds of thousands. A new Competition Commission inquiry backs up what many doctors and patients have been saying for years. Carte Blanche takes a dive into the world of medical care to find out what's going wrong.
metadata.Summary: Anyone who can afford to, pays ever-increasing medical aid premiums as a safety net for the day that the worst happens and you are diagnosed with cancer or a chronic condition. 16% of the South African population is covered by private medical aid care. In 1998 legislation was gazetted to implement Prescribed Minimum Benefits: a list of chronic, emergency and acute conditions which must be covered in full for any patient who is on a medical aid. This was supposed to be just the beginning of a series of policies to regulate the medical aid industry, but 20 years later the list has never been updated and neither have the treatment protocols. To make matters worse, most medical aid companies fail to inform their members that their conditions should be covered as PMBs. The result is patients paying extortionate medical expenses out of pocket, often when they are already incapacitated by illness. And for the rest of us, rising premiums making medical aid care ever less affordable and less comprehensive.
metadata.Further information: How the medical aid system works: the intention is that healthy and younger members subsidise older and sicker ones. We all pay our premiums; part of them is set aside for your savings pocket, to be used by you for everyday expenditure at your discretion. The rest is put into a risk pool, from which PMB expenses are paid. If you are diagnosed with a PMB condition, you are usually required to apply for a PMB benefit, but medical aid companies also have a legal obligation to proactively advise members that they qualify. However, patients frequently pay their PMB medical expenses out of their savings accounts, which are rapidly depleted, and are none the wiser about the systems that should be supporting them. In 2013, the Competition Commission approved an investigation into anti-competitive behaviour within the medical aid scheme industry. The preliminary Health Market Inquiry report, released earlier this year, found that: - there has been a chronic failure of implementation by the Department of Health, CMS and other regulators in the industry, and intended revisions and additions to the legislation have not been implemented since 2000 - the market is characterised by rising costs and disempowered consumers who are not adequately informed to navigate the system - private healthcare expenditure is high and has been increasing at a rate above CPI - lack of clarity on PMB cover amongst both healthcare practitioners and members means that treatment is a matter of trial and error; and the drive to access coverage means doctors might prescribe unnecessarily expensive treatment, or admit patients to hospital unnecessarily. - there are no mechanisms to ensure compliance by medical aids on PMB payments - prices are high because before 2004 tariffs were decided by collective bargaining; thereafter by inflation which never corrected for the excessive costs in 2004 when the change happened. - The WHO found that South Africa has one of the most expensive private healthcare systems in the world - At every step, it is patients and medical aid scheme members who bear the brunt of increasing costs and lowering coverage.
